title: networking-streaming-http-grpc-chunking-benchmarks
summary: Benchmarks comparing HTTP vs gRPC streaming for the serving runtime focusing on chunking strategies, backpressure behavior, and proxy effects (Envoy). Purpose is to quantify latency/throughput tradeoffs and produce actionable config recommendations for hosted and dedicated deployments.
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures iterative experiments and analysis on networking and streaming overheads for our GPU-backed serving runtime. We specifically compare HTTP chunked streaming vs gRPC streaming, measure impact of chunk size, transport-level buffering/backpressure, and effects introduced by edge proxies (Envoy) and an internal sidecar. The end goal is practical guidance for default SDK chunking, Envoy config, and canary checks for networking regressions.

Scope and non-goals:
- Focus: text-generation streaming path (token-by-token or micro-batched token flushes).
- Not covered: model execution time, kernel-level optimizations, or client-side rendering costs (except where they affect perceived latency).
- Environments: tests run on Dedicated-like instances (NVIDIA A100 equivalent), simulated client fleet in same region and cross-region. Also ran minimal tests on Hosted infra to confirm patterns.

Test rig (hardware/software):
- Serving: 2-node pool, each node: 8 vCPUs, 32GB RAM, 1x A100 (dev env).
- Clients: 16 worker VMs (4 vCPU, 8GB) generating concurrent sessions.
- Proxy: Envoy v1.25 as sidecar in front of each runtime; also direct path (no proxy) for baseline.
- Network: intra-region 1Gbps emulation for some runs (tc/netem used to add latency/loss).
- SDKs: HTTP/1.1 chunked via our rest-sdk; gRPC streaming via our proto + grpc-go (1.60) with http2 keepalive defaults.
- Load generator: custom harness (github link in linked_artifacts) that simulates user typing with configurable token emission cadence, and can generate bursty vs steady input.

Methodology:
- Requests: 1k unique sessions per run; each session requests generation of 256 tokens. We test two token flush patterns: per-token flush (emit every token as generated) and micro-batch flush (emit every 8 tokens).
- Concurrency sweep: 1, 5, 20, 50, 100 concurrent sessions sustained for 120s warmup + 300s measurement.
- Chunk sizes evaluated: per-token (~single token payload), 4-token, 8-token, 16-token. For HTTP chunked we control flush frequency; for gRPC we control stream send frequency.
- Measurements recorded: p50/p90/p99 of first-byte latency (time from request to first token), end-to-end completion latency, throughput (tokens/sec), network bytes on wire, CPU usage (user+sys), socket queue sizes, and observed application-level backpressure events (request queue growth, per-session stall time).
- Each experiment repeated 3x; median taken.

Key results (high level):
1) Latency: gRPC streaming p50 first-byte is consistently ~5-8ms lower than HTTP/1.1 chunked for per-token flush across all concurrencies (measured intra-region with no envoy). p99 gap grows with concurrency (gRPC p99 ~ 15-25ms lower than HTTP).
2) Throughput: at high concurrency (>=50 sessions) HTTP chunked achieves slightly higher aggregate tokens/sec when using 16-token micro-batches due to fewer syscalls and fewer small write syscalls. However, token-level freshness suffers.
3) Chunking tradeoff: switching from per-token->8-token micro-batch reduces network packets and CPU syscalls leading to 20-35% less CPU for network handling and up to 25% lower bytes-on-wire (less framing overhead). Latency p50 increases roughly linearly with batch size (per-token->8-token adds ~6-12ms median depending on model token generation speed).
4) Backpressure behavior: gRPC streaming's HTTP/2 flow-control provides smoother backpressure; clients see fewer application-level stalls. HTTP/1.1 chunked on some OS/socket stacks produced head-of-line blocking under ephemeral socket buffer exhaustion, causing session-level stalls visible in the request queue.
5) Envoy impact: adding Envoy sidecar adds ~3-6ms median latency for gRPC and ~6-12ms for HTTP chunked. When Envoy's max_connection_duration and HTTP/1.1 connection reuse settings were default, we observed additional p99 spikes due to Envoy re-establishing upstream connections under bursty workloads.
6) Cross-region: inter-region runs amplify differences; gRPC performs better for small-chunk streaming because it amortizes the round-trip via flow-control and header compression (HPACK/HTTP2), while HTTP chunked per-token is dominated by per-chunk framing and TCP push costs.

Representative numbers (intra-region, median of runs):
- Per-token flush, concurrency=20:
  - gRPC: first-byte p50=12ms, p90=28ms, p99=62ms; throughput=9.1k tokens/s total
  - HTTP chunked: first-byte p50=19ms, p90=42ms, p99=110ms; throughput=8.7k tokens/s total
- 8-token micro-batch, concurrency=50:
  - gRPC: first-byte p50=23ms, p90=45ms, p99=95ms; throughput=29k tokens/s
  - HTTP chunked: first-byte p50=28ms, p90=62ms, p99=180ms; throughput=31k tokens/s
- With Envoy in the path (same as 8-token, concurrency=50):
  - gRPC: p50 +4ms, p99 +18ms (increase observed)
  - HTTP: p50 +8ms, p99 +40ms (more sensitive to proxy config)

Observations & interpretation:
- gRPC streaming gives better tail latency due to HTTP/2 multiplexing and smoother flow-control; this matters for interactive experiences where p99 latency is user-visible.
- HTTP chunked with aggressive micro-batching is more efficient for throughput-first workloads (bulk embedding generation, non-interactive batch flows).
- Envoy misconfiguration (short upstream connection timeouts, aggressive HTTP/1.1 connection closing) is a major source of p99 spikes for HTTP chunked. Tuning keepalives and connection pool sizes mitigates most of that.
- On many OS kernels, small repeated writes (per-token) cause syscalls that dominate CPU at scale. Offloading to batching or using writev helps.

Recommendations (practical):
1) Default SDK behavior: use gRPC streaming for interactive streaming endpoints. Fall back to HTTP chunked when gRPC is not available (e.g., constrained clients), but use 4-token micro-batching by default in that case.
2) Server-side defaults: enable HTTP/2 with tuned flow-control limits for gRPC; set reasonable MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS to avoid head-of-line resource contention.
3) Envoy config: (a) prefer HTTP/2 upstream where possible, (b) set upstream connection pool max connections >= 2x expected concurrency per worker, (c) increase upstream idle/keepalive thresholds to avoid churn for bursty sessions.
4) Chunking policy: recommend client-configurable chunk target window (default 8 tokens), with adaptive mode that flushes earlier on low-latency environments and increases batch size under high CPU/network pressure.
5) Monitoring: add per-route metrics for socket write latency, per-session stall time, envoy upstream connection churn, and rate of application-level stall events. Add synthetic canary test that simulates per-token typing to catch regressions in tail latency.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Evaluate HTTP/2 over direct HTTP libraries (non-gRPC) - we tested only HTTP/1.1 chunked vs gRPC. Some client ecosystems support raw HTTP/2 with server-sent events; run a small comparison.
- Quantify cost impact: translate CPU/network savings from batching into $/M tokens delta for Hosted SKU.
- Test with TLS termination at different points (edge LB vs sidecar) - we saw some p99 differences depending on where TLS was terminated.

Commands / how to reproduce (notes for the perf harness):
- See linked_artifacts (github) for harness. Typical run: ./perf-harness --mode streaming --transport grpc --batching per-token --concurrency 50 --duration 420 --target serving-pool:443
- For Envoy: use envoy-perf.yaml (in repo) with connection pool tunables and run with /bin/envoy -c envoy-perf.yaml

Appendix: quick checklist for release/devops
- [ ] SDK: flip default to gRPC streaming for new SDK 2.x if platform support covers >= 95% of customers.
- [ ] Add server-side telemetry (stall_time_ms, per-session queue depth).
- [ ] Update Envoy default config in private-deployments to include tuned upstream connection pool and longer keepalives.
- [ ] Create canary job in Redwood Console that runs the per-token typing sim and alerts on p99 regressions >20ms vs baseline.

Notes to reviewers:
- Numbers are environment-dependent; absolute values will vary on different cloud providers and instance sizes. The relative differences and qualitative behaviors are robust across multiple testbeds executed in this project.
- If we decide to push gRPC streaming as default, need to confirm SDK language coverage and fallback logic for browsers / limited runtimes (WebSockets + HTTP chunking).

Raw experiment artifacts and raw data shipped to perf bucket; see github link for exact run IDs and CSVs.
